insider_note: This is one of the simplest separable equations in the chapter — y dy and x dx integrate to the same power-rule form on both sides, so the result is a family of circles centred at the origin.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Move x across, then multiply through by dx to separate the two variables.
steps.memory_tip: y·dy/dx = −x rearranges instantly to y dy = −x dx — one of the simplest separations in the chapter.
steps.why: Moving x to the other side and multiplying through by dx leaves y dy on the left and −x dx on the right, which is already fully separated with nothing further to rearrange.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign when moving x across, writing y dy = x dx instead of y dy = −x dx.
Dividing by y to get dy/dx = −x/y and then integrating the right-hand side with respect to x as if y were a constant — y still depends on x, so that integration is not valid.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. ∫y dy = y²/2 and ∫x dx = x²/2 by the power rule; combine and relabel the constant.
steps.memory_tip: y² + x² = 2c is a family of circles centred at the origin — one circle for each value of c, all sharing that centre.
steps.why: Integrating each side by the power rule gives y²/2 and −x²/2 respectively; multiplying the whole equation by 2 and relabelling the arbitrary constant gives the tidy family y² + x² = 2c.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to multiply through by 2, leaving fractions in the final answer as y²/2 + x²/2 = c.
Dropping the factor of 2 that appears when 2c is relabelled, and writing y² + x² = c instead.
